title: Seat a swivelling ball stud square in a knuckle's tapered hole, from a tie rod that swings
instruction: Lift the outer end of the tie rod off its wooden block, hold its swinging ball stud upright over the steering knuckle's tapered hole, and push the stud straight down until its taper seats in the hole, then let go.
context: ATRO Steer King Universal Tie Rods, Installation Instructions, step 7: "Insert a stud into the tapered hole of the Steering Knuckle. Install the Castle Nut loosely on the thread." Step 1 gives the cost of a bad seat: a hole "damaged or oblong/oval, allowing the new stud to rock in the hole" means the knuckle must be replaced, and "may result in a stud fracture and partial loss of steering." (a truck tie rod there, a car's outer tie rod end here) https://www.atrobushing.com/documents/EN-Steer-King-Tie-Rods-Installation-Instructions.pdf Done by: automotive and truck service technicians (steering and suspension).
setup: The two arm bases stand 61 cm apart on an oak table. The left end of a car's steering rack is fixed 25 cm out from the bases and 12 cm left of the midline: an aluminium tube 44 mm across on a 50 x 100 mm stand, with a rubber boot. A steel tie rod, 16 mm across and 36 cm long, hangs from the rack's inner ball joint 14.1 cm above the table and runs to the right. Near its outer end it rests level on a wooden block, 40 x 30 x 130 mm, 17 cm right of the midline. The outer tie rod end is a black body 22 mm across and a socket housing 40 mm across and 35 mm tall, 24 cm right of the midline, with a steel ball stud hanging straight down from it on its ball. The stud's taper is 18.0 mm across at its large end and 14.7 mm at its small end over 19.3 mm, with a 13.5 mm thread 22 mm long below. The stud swivels up to 20 degrees each way about two axes, and the tie rod turns up, down and sideways on the inner joint. The moving parts weigh 170 g. A fixed cast-iron steering knuckle has its hole 31.9 cm out and 23.3 cm right: an upright 30 x 80 x 140 mm and a steering arm, 24 x 16 mm, ending in a boss 44 mm across with a tapered hole that matches the stud, its axis upright and its top 90.6 mm above the table.
scoring: Seated: the stud's taper large end within 1 mm of the hole's axis and within 0.5 mm of its home depth (0.6 mm below the hole's top), and the stud's axis within 2 degrees of the hole's. 1.0 when the stud is seated and still (its taper and the tie rod's outer end under 0.01 m/s, both under 0.5 rad/s) for 1 s, which ends the trial. 0.6 when seated at the last step but still moving. 0.3 when the threaded tip is at least 2 mm below the hole's top, the stud's axis is within 2.42 mm of the hole's at the hole's top, it is no deeper than seated and within 2 degrees of upright. 0 otherwise: beside the hole, on its rim, cocked more than 2 degrees, dropped, or at the start. The scorer does not check the grasp or the release: a stud held seated by the gripper scores the same as one let go.
reset_notes: Lift the stud out of the knuckle, let it hang straight down, and lay the tie rod's outer end back on its block.
fidelity: Taper as four short cylinders just inside the cone, hole as 24 flat segments: the stud seats 0.6 mm deeper than flush. Each ball joint is two damped hinges; the stud lags and settles but has no preload (real socket bearings "maintain preload"). 170 g moving, against about 1.2 kg solid steel. Knuckle fixed, friction 1.2/1.0; stud 0.5/0.4. No nut or thread. Rod length, ball to taper, swivel range, thread length, housing and knuckle body are estimates.
scores: Dream-1 run: 0 (2,400 steps, on the earlier fixture, before the stud's 15 mm neck cylinder was given a positive height; nothing else in the scene changed); demo: 1.0 (success at 21.1 s)
